book_title: Chapter 1: From ResCare Roll-Up to Pure-Play Specialty & Home Care Platform
question: How did a Louisville-based residential disability care operator merge with an institutional pharmacy giant under KKR and Walgreens, survive a bruising leveraged balance sheet, and reinvent itself as a focused specialty pharmacy and home health platform?

epigraph.quote: We have a differentiated company, our value proposition for healthcare stakeholders is clear, and our confidence in the future remains high, supported by a broad set of process and growth drivers across a uniquely scaled and high-quality platform.
epigraph.author: Jon Rousseau, Chairman, President & CEO, BrightSpring Health Services (Q3 2026 Earnings Release)

web_blocks.title: 1.1 Corporate Lineage: ResCare, PharMerica, and the 2019 KKR–Walgreens Merger

web_blocks.html: BrightSpring Health Services, Inc. (NASDAQ: BTSG) is headquartered in Louisville, Kentucky. The company grew out of a deliberate private equity consolidation aimed at complex, high-cost patients outside hospital walls [1, 6]. Its operational roots trace back to Res-Care, Inc. (ResCare), founded in 1974 and taken private by Onex Corporation in 2004 [6]. ResCare built a national footprint in community residential support for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD), alongside home care and rehab [6]. Meanwhile, PharMerica Corporation spun out of AmerisourceBergen and Kindred Healthcare in 2007 [6]. It operated one of the largest institutional and long-term care (LTC) pharmacy networks in the United States [6].

In December 2017, private equity firm KKR & Co. and minority partner Walgreens Boots Alliance (WBA) acquired PharMerica Corporation [6]. Fifteen months later, in March 2019, the KKR–Walgreens consortium bought BrightSpring Health Holdings Corp., ResCare's parent entity [6]. They merged the two organizations under the BrightSpring Health Services banner [6]. The thesis was straightforward. Management wanted to pair high-touch home and community clinical services with a scaled pharmacy engine [6, 9]. That engine combined PharMerica's institutional base with its fast-growing oncology specialty unit, Onco360, to serve patients across the post-acute continuum [6, 9].

web_blocks.title: 1.2 The January 2024 IPO, Debt Overhang, and Sponsor Exit Arc

web_blocks.html: Five years of private equity ownership brought steady tuck-in deals and heavy debt service [6]. BrightSpring debuted on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on January 26, 2024 [6]. The IPO raised more than $1.04 billion in combined net proceeds across two concurrent offerings [6]. Common stock sales of 53,333,334 shares brought in $656.5 million net [6]. Another 8,000,000 6.75% Tangible Equity Units (TEUs) raised $389 million net [6]. Management used nearly all proceeds to pay down term loans [6]. At the same time, BrightSpring issued roughly $100 million in restricted stock units to about 20,000 frontline and tenured staff [6].

Even after the IPO, BrightSpring entered 2024 with two major overhangs. Net leverage sat above 3x to 4x, and KKR held over 50% alongside Walgreens' minority stake [6, 7]. Both overhangs unwound rapidly over 2025 and 2026. Walgreens Boots Alliance sold its remaining shares in the open market [7]. KKR then executed three orderly secondary offerings [7]. It sold 14.0 million shares in June 2025 and 15.0 million shares in October 2025 alongside a 1.5 million share company buyback [7]. In June 2026, KKR sold 14.67 million shares alongside up to $60 million in company repurchases [7]. Those sales cut KKR's indirect stake to about 27.15 million shares, or ~13.7% of shares outstanding [7].

web_blocks.title: 1.3 Portfolio Transformation: Divesting Community Living & Acquiring Amedisys/LHC Branches

web_blocks.html: BrightSpring's defining public-company pivot was shedding labor-heavy residential IDD group homes [5, 8]. Management chose to double down on higher-growth specialty pharmacy and home health instead [5, 8]. In January 2025, BrightSpring agreed to sell its legacy ResCare Community Living business to Sevita for $835 million in cash [5]. The deal faced a 14-month Federal Trade Commission (FTC) antitrust review [5]. To resolve that review, Sevita agreed to divest 128 intermediate care facilities in Indiana, Louisiana, and Texas to Dungarvin Group [5]. The sale closed on March 30–31, 2026 [5]. BrightSpring collected $811 million in net pre-tax proceeds (~$715 million after taxes) and paid down debt [2, 5]. Net leverage fell from 2.99x at year-end 2025 to 2.27x in Q1 2026 and 1.79x by September 30, 2026 [2, 4, 5].

At the same time, BrightSpring bought assets from an industry antitrust divestiture [8]. To clear UnitedHealth Group/Optum's $3.3 billion purchase of Amedisys, the Department of Justice (DOJ) required Optum to sell 164 home health and hospice sites across 19 states [8]. In Q4 2025, BrightSpring acquired 107 of those Amedisys and former LHC Group branches for about $239 million [8]. That deal nearly doubled BrightSpring's home health footprint from 14 states to roughly 30 states [8]. Branches clustered densely across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic [8]. As a result, Q3 2026 home health average daily census surged 58% year-over-year [2, 8].

Selling ResCare Community Living did more than shrink debt [1, 5]. It reshaped BrightSpring's labor, regulatory, and capital profile [1, 5]. Residential IDD group homes need 24/7 direct-support staffing, physical leases, and state-by-state Medicaid rate lobbying [5, 6]. Those sites face constant wage inflation and state budget swings [5, 6]. By transferring them to Sevita for $835 million ($811 million net pre-tax, ~$715 million after tax), BrightSpring shed a heavy operating drag [5]. Management also retired the legacy PharMerica 'Silver' False Claims Act case for $120 million in mid-2024 [1, 10]. Together, those steps cleared two persistent drains on cash flow and executive focus [1, 5, 10].

Governance also shifted from a controlled LBO subsidiary toward a broadly held public company [6, 7]. Walgreens exited completely, and three KKR secondary sales cut KKR's stake from over 50% to ~27.15 million shares (~13.7%) [6, 7]. Public float liquidity grew as sponsor ownership fell [6, 7]. Meanwhile, the IPO-era $100 million RSU grant helped retain about 20,000 tenured clinicians, pharmacists, and staff [6]. Becoming an independent operator freed capital allocation from legacy cross-holding constraints [2, 6, 8]. Management retired high-cost term loans and reinvested selectively in dense home health corridors [2, 6, 8]. As CEO Jon Rousseau noted in Q3 2026, BrightSpring now runs with 'a broad set of process and growth drivers across a uniquely scaled and high-quality platform' [2].

web_blocks.takeaway: Between 2024 and 2026, BrightSpring executed a textbook post-LBO transformation: monetizing its legacy residential IDD business for $835M, buying 107 DOJ-divested home health branches at a discount, and cutting net leverage to 1.79x [2, 5, 8].

web_blocks.mechanism: In August 2019, Walgreens Boots Alliance and Madison Dearborn Partners merged Option Care Enterprises with publicly traded BioScrip. The deal created the largest independent U.S. home and alternate-site infusion provider, reaching 96% of the U.S. population across 46 states. Like BrightSpring, the combined company started with heavy merger debt and thin margins. It then used national payer contracting, drug buying scale, and high-acuity chronic therapies to expand EBITDA and cut debt.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Post-merger scale across 46 states and >2,900 clinicians enabled Option Care Health to grow revenue past $5B+ while reducing net leverage from >5x at closing to under 2.0x within five years [14].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Option Care Health proves that a PE-backed, Walgreens-affiliated specialty/infusion roll-up can transition from a leveraged public debut into a durable cash-generative compounder—provided it sheds low-margin legacy assets and lets specialty drug mix drive operating leverage.

book_paragraphs: To understand BrightSpring Health Services, we have to look past the corporate name. We need to trace the two very different businesses bolted together in a Louisville boardroom in 2019. On one side sat ResCare, a fifty-year-old operator of group homes, personal care, and rehab services. ResCare's roots went back to 1974, and Onex Corporation took it private in 2004. On the other side sat PharMerica, a large institutional pharmacy network spun out of AmerisourceBergen and Kindred Healthcare in 2007. PharMerica served nursing homes and assisted-living sites, with a fast-growing oncology specialty gem called Onco360 tucked inside. KKR and Walgreens Boots Alliance bought PharMerica in December 2017. Fifteen months later, in March 2019, they bought ResCare and fused the two into BrightSpring.

Why did KKR and Walgreens put those two businesses under one roof? In theory, both served complex, high-cost patients outside hospital walls. In practice, their economics looked nothing alike. Group homes for adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) needed 24-hour staffing, physical real estate leases, and constant state Medicaid rate talks. Dispensing $15,000-a-month oral cancer drugs through Onco360 was an asset-light clinical logistics business. For five years under private equity, the marriage looked like a classic leveraged roll-up. BrightSpring made steady tuck-in deals, carried heavy term-loan interest, and ran a sprawling portfolio that public investors struggled to value.

BrightSpring came public on the Nasdaq in January 2024. The IPO raised just over $1.04 billion across 53.33 million common shares ($656.5 million net) and 8 million 6.75% Tangible Equity Units ($389 million net). Skeptics saw a debt-heavy LBO orphan trying to pay down term loans while KKR and Walgreens still owned over half the stock. Management granted roughly $100 million in restricted stock units to about 20,000 frontline nurses, pharmacists, and tenured staff. That move was smart for retention, yet it could not erase market doubts about a 3x-to-4x levered conglomerate.

What happened over the next thirty-three months ranks among the cleanest portfolio resets in modern healthcare services. First, management settled the legacy PharMerica 'Silver' False Claims Act case for roughly $120 million in mid-2024. That payout crushed FY2024 operating cash flow to $23.8 million, yet it stopped the past from ambushing future quarters. Second, in January 2025, CEO Jon Rousseau agreed to sell the entire ResCare Community Living unit to Sevita for $835 million in cash. The deal faced a grueling fourteen-month FTC antitrust review. Regulators required Sevita to divest 128 intermediate care facilities across Indiana, Louisiana, and Texas to Dungarvin Group. When the sale closed on March 30–31, 2026, BrightSpring collected $811 million in net pre-tax cash (about $715 million after taxes) and sent nearly all of it to debt reduction.

Look at the capital-allocation symmetry of what happened next. While BrightSpring shed labor-heavy group homes, the Department of Justice forced UnitedHealth Group's Optum unit to divest 164 home health and hospice sites across 19 states. That divestiture cleared Optum's $3.3 billion purchase of Amedisys. BrightSpring stepped into that forced-seller window in Q4 2025. It bought 107 of those Amedisys and former LHC Group branches for roughly $239 million. In one move, BrightSpring nearly doubled its home health footprint from 14 states to about 30, clustering across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic. Q3 2026 home health average daily census jumped 58% year-over-year. Rarely does a management team sell a slower, labor-heavy asset for $835 million and put less than a third of the cash into higher-return branches from a forced seller.

At the same time, the sponsor overhang that worried early public buyers steadily faded. Walgreens Boots Alliance sold its remaining shares on the open market. KKR executed three orderly secondary sales: 14.0 million shares in June 2025, 15.0 million in October 2025 with a 1.5 million share company buyback, and 14.67 million in June 2026 with up to $60 million in repurchases. Those sales trimmed KKR's stake to roughly 27.15 million shares, or ~13.7%. Combined with the Community Living cash, net leverage fell from 2.99x at year-end 2025 to 2.27x in Q1 2026 and 1.79x by September 30, 2026. As CEO Jon Rousseau stated in the Q3 2026 release, 'We have a differentiated company, our value proposition for healthcare stakeholders is clear, and our confidence in the future remains high.'

Notice the structural parallel with Option Care Health, which serves as a useful template. In August 2019, Walgreens and Madison Dearborn Partners merged Option Care with BioScrip to form a national home-infusion leader. The combined firm reached 96% of the U.S. population across 46 states with over 2,900 clinicians. Like BrightSpring, Option Care began its public life under >5x merger debt and skeptical analysts. Many doubted a thin-margin infusion roll-up could ever deleverage. Five years later, national payer contracts and chronic-therapy mix lifted revenue past $5 billion and cut leverage below 2.0x. Option Care turned into a durable compounder. BrightSpring is running that same playbook, paired with an even faster specialty oncology engine in Onco360.

Pause and ask why most post-LBO healthcare roll-ups stumble where BrightSpring succeeded. Usually, private equity sponsors load a firm with debt, cut frontline staff to dress up IPO EBITDA, and leave public buyers with high clinician turnover. BrightSpring did the opposite. It issued $100 million of IPO-era equity grants to 20,000 frontline nurses, pharmacists, and tenured staff. It swallowed the $120 million Silver settlement in year one instead of dragging litigation out. And it waited patiently through a fourteen-month FTC review to exit residential group homes cleanly for $835 million in cash.

Put all of Chapter 1 together and the strategic arc is clear. Between January 2024 and late 2026, BrightSpring moved from a debt-heavy, sponsor-controlled conglomerate into a focused, sub-2x-levered specialty pharmacy and home health platform across roughly 30 states. Every major move—settling Silver, selling Community Living to Sevita, buying 107 DOJ-divested Amedisys and LHC branches, and absorbing three KKR secondaries—pushed the business up the quality curve.

book_callouts.title: The Post-LBO Clean-Up Checklist
book_callouts.text: When private equity sponsors take a healthcare roll-up public, the first two years tell you whether management is playing offense or just servicing debt. In BrightSpring's case, selling Community Living for $835M while buying 107 DOJ-divested Amedisys/LHC branches for $239M cut net leverage from 2.99x to 1.79x in nine months—a rare example of simultaneously simplifying the story and upgrading asset quality.
